blocks.text: Sulfur usually forms single bonds with other sulfur atoms instead of double bonds, because of the poor overlap of its orbitals. As a result it forms larger molecules and structures through catenation: S8 is a crown-like molecule (Figure 12.7). This bonding, and the stability of its compounds, explains the low reactivity of sulfur at room temperature.

blocks.prompt: Why is sulfur quite unreactive at room temperature (exercise Q.2g)?
blocks.explanation: Sulfur exists as stable S8 crown rings held by strong S-S single bonds; because 3p orbitals overlap poorly sideways it does not form the reactive double bonds that oxygen does. Breaking the rings needs energy, so sulfur reacts only when heated, as when it burns to SO2.

items: Sulfur prefers S-S single bonds (poor orbital overlap), catenates into rings and chains; S8 is a crown-shaped molecule; hence low reactivity at room temperature.
